introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - Ordinary Level Examination. Computer Science (0595), Paper 3 (practical), June 2025. Duration: two and a half hours. Do all the tasks (Task I, Task II, Task III) specified in this question paper.**

The booklet reproduced here contains four versions of the same practical paper, headed Group One, Group Two, Group Three and Group Four (booklets 00/0595/3/Grp 1, Grp 2, Grp 3 and Grp 4). Each version has three tasks: Task I (word processing, 20 marks), Task II (spreadsheet, 20 marks) and Task III (reading and running a short C or Pascal program, 10 marks). A candidate works on one group only.

Enter the information required in the shaded boxes. For your guidance, the approximate mark for each part of a question is indicated in brackets. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. All written answers should be provided in the spaces provided in this question booklet. Calculators are NOT allowed.

The working files named in the tasks (documents, workbooks and pictures supplied in the candidate folder) are supplied on the day; they are not reproduced in the printed paper.

Le sujet imprime un tableau de deux exécutions ; la valeur de la hauteur de Mary à la seconde exécution est imprimée « 1,5 » avec une virgule (probable faute de frappe pour 1.5) : le corrigé la lit 1.5 (avec une virgule, scanf lirait 1 puis échouerait et le readln du Pascal ferait une erreur d'exécution). Le `readln()` final du Pascal est imprimé avec des parenthèses vides (accepté par les compilateurs courants, non conforme à l'ISO strict). Points imprimés : 3 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 10, comme l'en-tête.

questions.enonce_markdown: Launch either a C or Pascal program development environment, and key in the corresponding program. Do not key in the line numbers, which have been provided for convenience. Compile the program. If any errors, keep correcting and compiling until the errors are all corrected. Save as Task 3.  *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Open a C or a Pascal development environment installed on the computer, create a new source file, key in the program of your choice **exactly as printed** without the line numbers, and compile it (*Build* / *Compile*, often F9). Save the file as **Task 3**.

- Check the details while typing: the `#include`, the semicolons and the braces in C; the doubled apostrophe in `Mary''s` and `John''s` in Pascal (a single apostrophe would end the string), the `&` before each variable in `scanf`, and `%f` for a float.
- If the compiler reports an error, go to the line indicated, correct it and compile again until there is no error.

*Marking idea (3 marks):* program keyed correctly (1); compiled without error (1); saved as Task 3 (1).

questions.enonce_markdown:
Run the program two times, with the following inputs, and write the last three output lines in each case.

| | First run | Second run |
|---|---|---|
| Mary's height in metres | 1.5 | 1.5 |
| Mary's weight in kilograms | 65 | 65 |
| John's height in centimetres | 160 | 150 |
| John's weight in grams | 70000 | 65000 |

Output for first run  *[2 marks]*

................

................

................
questions.corrige_markdown:
First run: Mary's BMI is 65 / (1.5 x 1.5) = 65 / 2.25 = 28.888... which is displayed with 2 decimal places as 28.89. John's data are converted first: 70000 g / 1000 = 70 kg and 160 cm / 100 = 1.6 m, so his BMI is 70 / (1.6 x 1.6) = 70 / 2.56 = 27.34375, displayed as 27.34 (simulated in Python, same results in single and double precision).

```
Body Mass Index
Mary: 28.89
John: 27.34
```

(A blank line comes before *Body Mass Index*: it is produced by the `\n` at the start of the string in C, or by `writeln;` in Pascal. The last three lines of the output are the three lines shown above.)

*Marking idea (2 marks):* title line and Mary's line (1); John's line (1).

Second run: Mary is the same as before (28.89). John: 65000 g / 1000 = 65 kg and 150 cm / 100 = 1.5 m, so his BMI is 65 / (1.5 x 1.5) = 65 / 2.25 = 28.888... displayed as 28.89.

```
Body Mass Index
Mary: 28.89
John: 28.89
```

*Marking idea (2 marks):* title line and Mary's line (1); John's line (1).

questions.enonce_markdown: Examine the output for the second run. How do John's and Mary's body mass index compare? Explain the results.  *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**John's and Mary's BMI are equal** (both 28.89). The two people have the same mass and the same height, only expressed in different units: Mary's data are in kilograms and metres (65 kg, 1.5 m) and John's in grams and centimetres (65000 g, 150 cm). The program converts John's values to the units of the formula before computing: `w2/1000` turns grams into kilograms (65000 g = 65 kg) and `h2/100` turns centimetres into metres (150 cm = 1.5 m). After the conversion both BMI are 65 / 1.5^2 = 28.89 kg/m$^2$. Without the conversions John's BMI would have been 65000 / 150^2 = 2.89 (wrong).

*Marking idea (3 marks):* the two BMI are equal (1); same mass and height in different units (1); the conversions by 1000 and by 100 explain it (1).
